title: Visualizations and the questions they answer (preview)

blocks.content: Explore finished dashboards on Grafana Play one panel at a time to see what each visualization is for and the question it answers. A stat shows a current value. A gauge or bar gauge shows how close a value is to a limit. A bar chart compares categories. A pie chart shows shares of a total. A table gives exact values, row by row.
Explore the panels that show one value and how the stat visualization displays it.
Open **Sample Website Dashboard**.
Find the **Support calls** panel. Like **Sign ups** beside it, it shows one large number. Each is a stat.
This panel answers the question: What is the current number of support calls? The faint line beneath the number sketches how the value moved, but the number is what the viewer takes in at a glance.
Focus on the **server requests** panel, a time series.

This panel answers the question: How has the number of requests gone up and down over time? A stat would reduce those samples to one number and hide the pattern. A stat suits a key metric to check at a glance. When the viewer needs the trend, a time series says more.
You've seen the stats on a dashboard and the question each one answers: one value to take in at a glance, where a time series shows the trend.
Explore a gauge and a bar gauge to see how each one shows a value within a range and answers "How close is the value to a limit?"
Open **Grafana Dashboard**.
Find the **Memory** gauge.
This panel answers the question: How close is memory use to its limit? The filled arc shows where the value sits within a range, which a value-only stat doesn't show.

The range comes from the panel's **Min** and **Max** settings under Standard options, 0 and 300 here. The endpoints don't have to appear as labels on the gauge. In this demo the range is a display setting, not a real memory capacity, so check where a gauge's limit comes from before trusting it.
Focus on the horizontal **Google hits** bar gauge.

This panel answers the same question for several values at once. Each bar's length shows its value's position within the range, a bar instead of an arc. Don't confuse it with a bar chart, which compares categories on a shared axis.
You've seen a gauge and a bar gauge show where a value sits within a configured range, and where that range comes from.
Explore a bar chart to see how it answers "How do the values for different categories compare with each other?"
Open **Bar charts and pie charts**.
Find the **Popular JS Frameworks** bar chart.
This panel answers the question: How do the values for different categories compare with each other? The library names are the categories, and the star counts supply the numeric values.

Stars, forks, and watchers are three different GitHub counts for each library's repository. The legend keeps the measure the same, so compare bars of one color. **Vue**'s green **Github Stars** bar is longer than **React.js**'s in this fixed sample, so Vue has more stars.
Bar lengths on a shared scale answer "Which included library has more stars?" Stars, forks, and watchers measure different actions, not how many people use each library.
You've seen a bar chart compare one numeric measure across categories. Next, the same star counts as shares of a total.
Explore a pie chart to see how it answers "How much of the total does each part make up?" and what that total includes.
Open **Bar charts and pie charts**.
Focus on the **Popular JS Frameworks** pie chart.
This panel answers the question: How much of the total does each part make up? **Vue**'s slice is larger than **React.js**'s because its star count is larger.
All six libraries' slices add to 100%. The whole is their combined star count, not all libraries, all developers, or all library usage.
The bar chart answers "Which count is larger?" The pie answers "What share of this included total does each count represent?" A pie fits here because the star counts add up to a total.
You've seen a pie chart show each part's share and what its total includes. Next, the row-level detail that summary charts leave out.
Explore a table to see how it answers "What are the exact values, row by row?" and what it lets you do that a chart doesn't.
Open **Visualizing Google Sheets Data**.
Find the **Top 50 Post Data** table.
Each row is one forum post. The column headings, **id**, **title**, **reply_count**, **views**, **last_posted_at**, **category_id**, and **status**, tell you what each cell holds.
The post with the most **views** is at the top. Its row gives you its **title**, **status**, and when it was last posted, all at once.

Click the **reply_count** heading. The rows re-sort by that column, descending first and ascending on the next click. The post with the most replies is a different post from the one with the most views.

Two posts with the same **status** can be compared view count by view count. A bar chart could show which bar is longer. Only the table gives you the exact numbers, with the title, date, and category beside them.
You've seen how a table gives exact values, row by row, and lets you sort them.
